extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent practitioners reading examiner guidance)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for identifying when claimed subject matter is an 'abstract idea' (especially the 'mental processes' and 'fundamental economic/commercial/social' groupings) and how to evaluate computer-implemented claims for patent eligibility. Meant to guide examiners in applying case law examples to claim analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental economic practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that recite fundamental economic principles or practices (e.g., hedging risk, managing insurance, mitigating settlement risk, rules for wagering, financial instruments designed to protect against investment risk).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such economic practices have been treated as unpatentable abstract ideas (e.g., Bilski v. Kappos — hedging; Bancorp — managing stable value protected life insurance; Alice — mitigating settlement risk). Examples include offer-based price optimization (OIP Techs. v. Amazon), local processing of payments for remotely purchased goods (Inventor Holdings v. Bed Bath Beyond), order placement based on displayed market information (Trading Technologies), and using markings on mail to communicate sender/recipient/content (Secured Mail Solutions). Examiner should recognize claims directed to these kinds of longstanding economic practices as abstract ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial or legal interactions
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims reciting commercial interactions or legal interactions such as agreements/contracts, legal obligations, advertising/marketing/sales activities, or business relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: transaction performance guaranty (buySAFE v. Google — contractual relationship), tax-free exchanges and real estate portfolio tools (Fort Properties), processing insurance claims under a policy (Accenture v. Guidewire), advertising-as-exchange (Ultramercial — displaying ads in exchange for access), structuring sales or marketing organizations (In re Ferguson), optimal visit algorithms for sales representatives (In re Maucorps), business relation systems for credit application and financing packages (Credit Acceptance v. Westlake), and processing through clearing-houses (Dealertrack v. Huber). Claims that are 'squarely about creating a contractual relationship' or other commercial/legal frameworks are often directed to abstract ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managing personal behavior or relationships or interactions between people
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that involve organizing human activity such as social activities, teaching, following rules or instructions, or otherwise managing personal behavior or interpersonal interactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: budgeting/tracking spending limits (Intellectual Ventures v. Capital One — tracking financial transactions to enforce pre-set spending limits), voting and vote verification (Voter Verified), attention managers that provide information without disrupting primary activity (Interval Licensing v. AOL), content filtering (BASCOM), considering historical usage while inputting data (BSG Tech v. Buyseasons), hair-design assignment by head shape (In re Brown), and dice-game wagering rules (In re Marco Guldenaar). Examiners should view claims that merely organize or manage ordinary human activities as abstract ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental processes (abstract idea grouping)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concepts performed in the human mind (thinking), including observations, evaluations, judgments, and opinions are grouped as 'mental processes' and treated as abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The courts consider a mental process that 'can be performed in the human mind, or by a human using a pen and paper' to be an abstract idea (CyberSource; Benson; Mayo; Parker v. Flook). This grouping covers both process and product claims that simply recite mental steps; examiners should evaluate whether claimed steps are the equivalent of human mental work (e.g., collecting information, analyzing it, comparing sequences, making determinations).

rubrics_metrics.name: A: Claims that cannot practically be performed in the human mind are not 'mental processes'
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim limitations cannot practically be performed in the human mind (i.e., humans are not equipped to perform them), the claim does not recite a mental process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of non-mental claims: calculating absolute GPS position and time using pseudoranges (SiRF Tech.); detecting suspicious network activity by using network monitors and analyzing packets (SRI Int'l); specific multi-step data encryption methods requiring complex data manipulation (Synopsys); rendering a halftone image by pixel-by-pixel comparison against a blue noise mask (Research Corp. Techs.). Examiners should identify whether the claimed operations are beyond human mental or pen-and-paper capabilities when deciding they are not 'mental processes.'

rubrics_metrics.name: B: Claims encompassing a human performing the steps mentally (with or without a physical aid) recite a mental process
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim can practically be performed wholly in a human mind, or by a human with a simple physical aid (e.g., pen and paper, slide rule), it falls within the mental processes grouping and is an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use cases: Benson (binary-coded decimal to binary conversion could be done mentally), CyberSource (constructing a map of credit card transactions could be done by writing down transactions), Synopsys (translating a functional description into a hardware description reads on an individual performing the steps mentally or with pencil and paper). The use of simple physical aids does not negate the mental nature of the limitation; examiners should consider specification disclosures that show steps are performable by humans with simple aids.

rubrics_metrics.name: C: Claims that require a computer may still recite a mental process
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that is implemented on a computer can nonetheless be an abstract idea if the underlying concept could be performed mentally (or is a human cognitive action).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supreme Court and Federal Circuit precedent (e.g., Benson, Mortgage Grader) show that computer implementation alone does not save an otherwise-mental concept. Examiners should review the specification and the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim to determine whether the applicant merely claims a concept performed on a generic computer, in a computer environment, or uses a computer as a tool. Examples: Voter Verified (voting, verifying, and submitting votes are human cognitive actions); Versata (pricing implemented on general purpose hardware). If the claim is just a human-performed concept on a generic computer, treat it as a mental-process abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate claims using broadest reasonable interpretation in light of the specification
rubrics_metrics.description: When deciding whether a computer-implemented claim recites a mental process, examiners should use the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim in view of the specification to see whether the claimed invention is described as a concept performed in the human mind or merely implemented on generic computer hardware.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifically, determine if the specification describes the claimed invention as: 1) a concept performed in the human mind, and the applicant merely claims it performed on a generic computer; 2) a concept performed in a computer environment; or 3) a concept where a computer is merely a tool to perform the concept. In such scenarios, the claim is considered to recite a mental process. The examination should consider specification descriptions of mental/pen-and-paper methodologies, flowsheets, or charts that indicate human-performable steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product and process claims can both recite mental-process abstract ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'mental processes' label refers to the type of abstract idea, not the statutory claim category; both product (e.g., systems, computer-readable media) and process claims may be directed to mental processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have identified product claims (e.g., computer systems, media) as reciting mental processes when the claimed functions read on human-performable mental steps (Versata; Intellectual Ventures v. Symantec; Mortgage Grader). Examiners should therefore not assume that claim drafting as a system or medium avoids the mental-process classification; analyze the substantive claimed steps and whether they are human mental work or equivalent.
